extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and critics/students of the novel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling point of view and the related methods of dramatization vs pictorial narration in writing fiction, including when to use scenes, oblique narration, first/third person choices, and how to prepare and economize dramatic material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view governs method
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole intricate question of method ... is governed by the question of the point of view — the question of the relation in which the narrator stands to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the method (dramatic, pictorial, mixed) based on the narrator's relation to the events; the subject dictates the method and the required effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a narrator-in-the-story to dramatize
rubrics_metrics.description: If the story-teller is in the story himself, the author is dramatized; his assertions gain in weight, for they are backed by the presence of the narrator in the pictured scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing a spokesman into the book shifts responsibility visibly onto a character-narrator, disguises arbitrary authorial voice, and can make the story self-contained. Best when the narrator has direct experience to relate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show events directly rather than reporting when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Not an account or a report, more or less convincing, is to be offered him, but a direct sight of the matter itself, while it is passing. Nobody expounds or explains; the story is enacted by its look and behaviour at particular moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the reader at the angle of vision so scenes are enacted in real time; this achieves dramatization and forestalls the narrator. Use when the subject benefits from immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the subject dictate how far to dramatize
rubrics_metrics.description: How far he may choose to push the process in his book — that is a matter to be decided by the subject; it entirely depends upon the kind of effect that the novelist desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide degree of dramatization vs narrative summary based on what effect the subject requires; avoid dogmatic adherence to one mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purely dramatic (scenic) form limits access to inner thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The purely dramatic subject ... never deviates from a strictly scenic form; in rigid drama of this kind there is naturally no admission of the reader into the private mind of any of the characters; their thoughts and motives are transmuted into action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strict scenic form for compact, authoritative effects where external action can carry the story; avoid when the story's burden is inward or panoramic in scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic scene is costly in time and space
rubrics_metrics.description: In the scene, it is clear, there can be no foreshortening of time or space ... It cannot cover more of either than it actually renders. And therefore it is, for its length, expensive in the matter of time and space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve dramatic scenes for moments that have been prepared for and that clinch or crown effects; do not squander scenes on material better served by summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (retrospective/narrative) method for panoramic or interior material
rubrics_metrics.description: In a pictorial book the principle of the structure involves a point of view which is not the reader's ... he must gather up his experience, compose a vision of it as it exists in his mind, and lay that before the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pictorial narration to cover long periods, panoramic surveys, or reflective material; it economy of time/space and accumulates impressions over stretches unsuitable for scenic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial can adopt dramatic techniques ('drama of the mind')
rubrics_metrics.description: In the drama of his mind there is no personal voice, for there is no narrator; the point of view becomes the reader's once more. The shapes of thought in the man's mind tell their own story. And that is the art of picture-making when it uses the dramatic method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pictorial narration is centered in consciousness, render the mind's moment-to-moment reactions (dramatic within a mind) to achieve vividness without abandoning retrospective form.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person narration fixes field of vision
rubrics_metrics.description: If he speaks in the first person there can, of course, be no uncertainty in the point of view; he has his fixed position, he cannot leave it. His description will represent the face that the facts in their sequence turned towards him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first person to constrain vision and guarantee consistency of perspective; recognize that it forbids the author externalizing that narrator's mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person oblique keeps character perspective while freeing time/manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: This limitation may have a convenience and a value in the story ... I But it need not be forfeited, it is clear, if the first/ person is changed to the third. The author may use the man's field of vision and keep as faithfully within it as though the man were speaking for himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use third-person tied to a character's vision to retain intimacy but allow the author temporal freedom (retrospect/present urgency) and subtle shifts in vantage without breaking identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of authorial and character perception to enrich scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: There are now two brains behind that eye; and one of them is the author's, who adopts and shares the position of his creature, and at the same time supplements his wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit subtle authorial supplementation of a character's perception (oblique narration) to add touches beyond the character's possible sensations, enriching the picture without breaking focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author may close the seer's consciousness to make the seer a dramatic actor
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero can at any moment become impenetrable, a human being whose thought is sealed from us; ... he drops into the plane of the people, he may mingle with the rest, engage in talk with them, and his presence and his talk are no more to the fore than theirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporarily suspend access to a focalizer's inner life to let them function as an ordinary dramatic character among others—this gives them objective weight and prevents them dissolving into a blur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting by a participant weakens pure drama
rubrics_metrics.description: When one of the people who took part in it sets out to report the scene, there is at once a mixture and a confusion of effects; for his own contribution to the scene has a different quality from the rest, cannot have the same crispness and freshness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid having a participant narrate a scene they acted in if the aim is to achieve the clean immediacy of drama; the report will inevitably differ in quality from the enacted parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not take the easiest (minstrel) way unless suited
rubrics_metrics.description: The old, immemorial ... way of telling a story, where the author entertains the reader, the minstrel draws his audience round him ... And if there is anyone who can proceed in this fashion without appearing to lose the least of the advantages of a more cautious style, for him the minstrel's licence is proper and appropriate;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial omniscience/minstrel voice is legitimate when it serves the story, but generally it is the easy way and typically narrows the story's possibilities; prefer disciplined method that makes the most of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: The novelist needs a working theory of relative uses of devices
rubrics_metrics.description: In the handling of his book a novelist must have some working theory, I suppose, to guide him — some theory of the relative uses and values of the different means at his disposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a conscious practice about when to use scene vs summary, first vs third person, oblique narration etc.; rely on consistent choices rather than haphazard mixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene should be used to clinch effects, not to do all the work
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene, therefore, all other effects will appear to be subordinated ... the placing of the scenes of the story will be the prime concern. But precisely because it has this high value it will need to be used prudently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenes primarily to deliver final strokes—clinch a matter already pending or crown an effect half-made by other means. Prepare scenes in advance; avoid wasting them on unprepared material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture (panoramic survey) complements drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture, the general survey, with its command of time and space, finds its opportunity where a long reach is more needed than sharp visibility ... Its office is to pile up an accumulated impression that will presently be completed by another agency, drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ panoramic narration to accumulate impressions across time/space, then deploy drama to realize and finalize those impressions; hold picture to its natural preparatory function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert pictorial thinness into strength by dramatizing the narrator's mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The inherent weakness is to be plainly admitted ... When you recall and picture an impression in words you give us ... a sight of things in a mirror ... Of the mirror, then, you may make a solid and defined and visible object; you may dramatize this thing at least, this mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using retrospective/pictorial method, make the narrator's mind itself a visible, dramatized object to gain intensity and avoid flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblique narration reduces insistence of narrator's voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The sound of the narrator's voice ... is less insistent in oblique narration, even while it seems to be following the very same argument that it would in direct, because another voice is speedily mixed and blended with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use oblique or indirect narration to soften dominant authorial tone, blend perspectives, and allow more than one 'eye' to inform the picture without confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the craft; criticism should be constructive and technical
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of criticism in the matter of fiction seems clear ... There is nothing more that can usefully be said about a novel until we have fastened upon the question of its making and explored it to some purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and writers should analyze how books are made—study technique (points of view, scene placement, methods) by reading constructively to recreate and understand the workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid squandering dramatic opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: They squander the scene; they are always ready to break into dialogue, into dramatic presentation, and often when there is nothing definitely to be gained by it; but they neglect the fully wrought and unified scene, amply drawn out and placed where it gathers many issues together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard dramatic material; prefer fully developed, multifunctional scenes over frequent shallow dramatic interruptions. Ensure every part of a scene advances the story without forced effort.
